intake: agnostic — seminary-trained, still think classical theism is the serious version of the question, cannot close the gap between a first cause and a God who acts, and have not settled it either way

walk.note: Biographically true for me and for nearly everyone; an inherited story is where the question first arrives.
The step from 'no evidence outside testimony' to 'texts appear written by man' is quicker than I'd like, but turning to natural theology is exactly the move I made.
The first-cause gap is enough to carry me to doubt; the closing clause is wrong, though — classical theism does not deny a God with intellect and will, it denies that God is one being among others.

The dilemma rests on 'a God who chooses is the personal God classical theism denies'; Aquinas's God has will and chooses, so a choosing, hidden God is not excluded and STEP tests a different hypothesis.
Granting no God, 'mind does not seem to reduce to matter' is a felt difficulty, not a reason for two kinds of thing; it leaves dualism open rather than reaching it.
Elisabeth's question is the real one, and the brain-dependence evidence does the work; I appreciate the honesty that Ryle's objection was a different one.
A terminological correction I agree with.
That physics describes only structure makes the intrinsic nature unknown, not mental; this needs an extra premise the text does not supply.
The reasoning wobbles (appealing to brains while inside Dream), but the conclusion is close enough to the cogito that I take it anyway.
Strawson's point stands regardless of how the previous move was reached.
The author says it is a choice, and it is the choice I would make.
Care ahead of proof keeping the unknown open is Socratic learned ignorance; the entropy aside is hard to place but does not hurt the move.
The author grants that acknowledged limits equally allow a secular hope; I would keep the hope and the fidelity without calling them faith toward a maker.
The move's own last sentence says being a maker does not make a maker resolved, which is the inference the move needs.
The text says only that it is more of a bargain than an argument; I cannot tell what the bargain is or who is bargaining.

'To think is to ignore' is true of finite attention, not shown for any possible mind; the author concedes Aquinas's single-act knowing has not been shown incoherent, and I take that concession seriously.
Suffering is bad for the sufferer whether or not anything stands behind it; I hold this myself and Parfit is the right citation.

I take it as arriving at the open question of personal continuity, which is the right next question, though the author herself says the need is motive and not evidence, so 'Dualism' is a misleading name.
I take it only in the sense that I agree this is where to stop: whether an outside can prove an inside is open and there is no data yet.

first_exit.why: The route's reason for leaving agnosticism is that a God who acts should show up in prayer statistics and that a God who chooses to hide is a 'subject' classical theism denies. The second half is false — the God of Aquinas has intellect and will — and once that goes, the prayer studies only rule out a vending-machine god, which is not the account I was doubting.

comment: You are honest to a fault in the second turn — moves 14, 15, and 16 each tell the reader, in their own words, that they do not establish what the position box claims — so let the position names carry that honesty too (Classical theism₂ should not say 'implies' when the move says it does not). And please check what classical theism actually denies: Aquinas's God chooses, so moves 3 and 4 need a different route out of theism than 'a God who chooses is a subject.' The first turn argues; the second turn chooses, and I respect that you say so.
